content:
In a new study, Apple researchers detailed SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model capable of jointly generating protein sequences and structures. Details below.

Some background

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled "SimpleFold: Folding Proteins is Simpler Than You Think," detailing a streamlined method for predicting three-dimensional protein structures from amino acid sequences.

In short, SimpleFold uses a flow matching model to directly generate 3D protein structures from amino acid sequences.

We've explained flow matching in detail before, but in brief, the technique starts from a noisy random point and learns a relatively direct path to the final result. This stands in contrast to diffusion models, which typically arrive at their final output through repeated denoising.

The most common (or at least historically most common) application of both techniques is image generation, though researchers (including Apple's researchers) have explored diffusion models for text and code generation as well.

Returning to SimpleFold, Apple essentially combined flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (commonly used for text generation), allowing the model to sidestep some of the more computationally expensive techniques found in traditional protein folding models (like DeepMind's famous AlphaFold).

Now, Apple researchers have introduced SimpleDesign, applying the simpler, more general architectural concepts explored in SimpleFold to the broader problem of protein design—not just predicting 3D protein structures.

SimpleDesign

As the Apple researchers explained in a new study titled "SimpleDesign: A Unified Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Co-Design":

In other words, while many existing protein design models rely on multi-stage pipelines, SimpleDesign learns to generate amino acid sequences and continuous 3D structures simultaneously in a single end-to-end training process.

Many existing co-design models work like this: first, they train a separate model to convert protein structures into discrete representations—so-called "tokens." Then, they train a generative model to operate on those representations in order to produce new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips this intermediate step, learning directly from paired amino acid sequences and 3D coordinates rather than first compressing protein structures into separate tokenized representations.

The Apple researchers trained SimpleDesign in a rather interesting way.

They started with a dataset of over 2 million paired protein sequences and structures, primarily drawn from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold database with other samples.

During training, they perturbed both parts of each pair: amino acids in the sequence were randomly masked behind mask tokens, while noise was added to the corresponding 3D structures.

The researchers also varied the degree of perturbation on both sides. If the sequence is largely intact but the structure is heavily corrupted, the task becomes similar to protein folding, requiring the model to recover the structure from a known sequence.

Conversely, if the structure is largely intact but the sequence is heavily masked, this resembles inverse folding—the model must generate a sequence that yields a given structure.

And when both are partially perturbed, the model learns to handle both problems at once, effectively being trained for protein co-design.

According to the study, SimpleDesign achieved competitive results on benchmarks for protein co-design, structure generation, and sequence generation, despite a notably simpler training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign was able to generate plausible protein structures, with its generated amino acid sequences generally on par with—and in some cases outperforming—those from most competing multimodal models.

Finally, the researchers noted that SimpleDesign's results remain limited to in silico evaluations, as the generated proteins have not yet been tested experimentally to confirm that they actually fold, function, or operate safely in real biological systems.

Still, these results are quite encouraging, and the full study (which naturally goes into much greater depth on SimpleDesign's architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results) is well worth a read.
